chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'May I be your ransom, regarding fish, which of them is permissible to eat?' He said, 'That which has a shell/skin.' I said, 'May I be your ransom, what do you say about the kanzat (a type of fish)?' He said, 'There is no harm in eating it.' I said, 'For it does not have a shell/skin.' He said, 'Yes, but it is a fish of bad character; it rubs itself against everything, so if you look at the base of its ear, you will find it has a shell/skin.'

key_terms.أُذُنِهَا: Its ear, the specific location where the shell is found for this fish
key_terms.الْكَنْعَتِ: A specific type of fish mentioned in the narration
key_terms.سَيِّئَةُ الْخُلُقِ: Bad character, used metaphorically to describe the fish's nature
key_terms.قِشْرٌ: Shell or skin, the primary criterion for permissible fish

ai.seo_question: What is the condition for a fish to be halal in Shia jurisprudence according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) refines the general juristic principle that permissible fish must possess a 'qishr' (shell or skin) by addressing the specific case of the 'kanzat'. He clarifies that while the kanzat lacks an external shell, it possesses one at the base of its ear, thereby validating its permissibility and demonstrating the nuanced application of biological observation in Shia fiqh. This narration highlights the tradition's reliance on precise physical characteristics to determine halal status, moving beyond superficial appearances to internal or hidden anatomical features.
